claim: Brain development relies on an interplay between genetic specification and self-organization.
source: Brain development relies on an interplay between genetic specification and self-organization.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the study's context.

claim: In the somatosensory brainstem, thalamus, and cortex of rats and mice, the arrangement of the facial whiskers is preserved in the arrangement of cell aggregates to form precise somatotopic maps.
source: Striking examples of this relationship can be found in the somatosensory brainstem, thalamus, and cortex of rats and mice, where the arrangement of the facial whiskers is preserved in the arrangement of cell aggregates to form precise somatotopic maps.
evidence: This is an established fact about whisker barrel organization in rodents, supported by existing scientific literature.

claim: Realistic whisker maps can self-organize by assuming that information is exchanged between adjacent cells only, under the guidance of gene expression gradients.
source: We show in simulation how realistic whisker maps can self-organize, by assuming that information is exchanged between adjacent cells only, under the guidance of gene expression gradients.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through computational simulations.

claim: Spatial patterns in neural connectivity provide clues about the constraints under which brains evolve and develop.
source: Spatial patterns in neural connectivity provide clues about the constraints under which brains evolve and develop (Purves et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Purves et al., 1992.

claim: The most distinctive pattern in neural connectivity can be found in the barrel cortex of many rodent species.
source: Perhaps the most distinctive pattern can be found in the barrel cortex of many rodent species (Woolsey and Van der Loos, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Woolsey and Van der Loos, 1970.

claim: Barrels are identifiable soon after birth in layer 4 of primary somatosensory cortex as dense clusters of thalamocortical axons.
source: The barrels are identifiable soon after birth in layer 4 of primary somatosensory cortex as dense clusters of thalamocortical axons, which are enclosed by borders a few neurons thick from postnatal day 3 (Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012.

claim: Barrels are enclosed by borders a few neurons thick from postnatal day 3.
source: The barrels are identifiable soon after birth in layer 4 of primary somatosensory cortex as dense clusters of thalamocortical axons, which are enclosed by borders a few neurons thick from postnatal day 3 (Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012.

claim: In the plane tangential to the cortical surface, the barrels constitute a somatotopic map of the whiskers.
source: In the plane tangential to the cortical surface the barrels constitute a somatotopic map of the whiskers, with cells within adjacent barrels responding most strongly and quickly to deflection of adjacent whiskers (Armstrong-James et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Armstrong-James et al., 1992.

claim: Cells within adjacent barrels respond most strongly and quickly to deflection of adjacent whiskers.
source: In the plane tangential to the cortical surface the barrels constitute a somatotopic map of the whiskers, with cells within adjacent barrels responding most strongly and quickly to deflection of adjacent whiskers (Armstrong-James et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Armstrong-James et al., 1992.

claim: Barrel patterning reflects subcortical whisker maps comprising cell aggregates called barrelettes in the brainstem and barreloids in the thalamus.
source: Barrel patterning reflects subcortical whisker maps comprising cell aggregates called barrelettes in the brainstem and barreloids in the thalamus (Ma, 1991; Van Der Loos, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma, 1991 and Van Der Loos, 1976.

claim: Barrel formation requires afferent input from whisker stimulation and thalamic calcium waves.
source: Barrel formation requires afferent input from whisker stimulation and thalamic calcium waves (Antón-Bolaños et al., 2019), and depends on a complex network of axon guidance molecules such as ephrin-A5 and A7 and adhesion molecules such as cadherin-6 and 8 (Vanderhaeghen et al., 2000; Miller et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Antón-Bolaños et al., 2019.

claim: Barrel formation depends on a complex network of axon guidance molecules such as ephrin-A5 and A7 and adhesion molecules such as cadherin-6 and 8.
source: Barrel formation requires afferent input from whisker stimulation and thalamic calcium waves (Antón-Bolaños et al., 2019), and depends on a complex network of axon guidance molecules such as ephrin-A5 and A7 and adhesion molecules such as cadherin-6 and 8 (Vanderhaeghen et al., 2000; Miller et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vanderhaeghen et al., 2000 and Miller et al., 2006.

claim: The network of axon guidance and adhesion molecules is orchestrated by interactions between morphogens Fgf8 and Fgf17 and transcription factors Emx2, Pax6, Sp8, and Coup-tf1.
source: This network is orchestrated by interactions between morphogens Fgf8 and Fgf17 and transcription factors Emx2, Pax6, Sp8, and Coup-tf1 (Shimogori and Grove, 2005; Bishop et al., 2000), which are expressed in gradients spanning the cortical sheet that mark orthogonal axes and can be manipulated to stretch, shrink, shift, and even duplicate barrels (Assimacopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shimogori and Grove, 2005 and Bishop et al., 2000.

claim: Morphogens and transcription factors are expressed in gradients spanning the cortical sheet that mark orthogonal axes.
source: This network is orchestrated by interactions between morphogens Fgf8 and Fgf17 and transcription factors Emx2, Pax6, Sp8, and Coup-tf1 (Shimogori and Grove, 2005; Bishop et al., 2000), which are expressed in gradients spanning the cortical sheet that mark orthogonal axes and can be manipulated to stretch, shrink, shift, and even duplicate barrels (Assimacopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shimogori and Grove, 2005 and Bishop et al., 2000.

claim: Gene expression gradients can be manipulated to stretch, shrink, shift, and even duplicate barrels.
source: This network is orchestrated by interactions between morphogens Fgf8 and Fgf17 and transcription factors Emx2, Pax6, Sp8, and Coup-tf1 (Shimogori and Grove, 2005; Bishop et al., 2000), which are expressed in gradients spanning the cortical sheet that mark orthogonal axes and can be manipulated to stretch, shrink, shift, and even duplicate barrels (Assimacopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Assimacopoulos et al., 2012.

claim: The barrel boundaries form a Voronoi tessellation.
source: The barrel boundaries form a Voronoi tessellation (Senft and Woolsey, 1991; Figure 1A), suggesting that barreloid topology is preserved in the projection of thalamocortical axons into the cortex, and that a barrel forms by lateral axon branching from an initial centre-point that ceases upon contact with axons branching from adjacent centres.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Senft and Woolsey, 1991 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Barreloid topology is preserved in the projection of thalamocortical axons into the cortex.
source: The barrel boundaries form a Voronoi tessellation (Senft and Woolsey, 1991; Figure 1A), suggesting that barreloid topology is preserved in the projection of thalamocortical axons into the cortex, and that a barrel forms by lateral axon branching from an initial centre-point that ceases upon contact with axons branching from adjacent centres.
evidence: This is an inference suggested by the Voronoi tessellation pattern.

claim: A barrel forms by lateral axon branching from an initial centre-point that ceases upon contact with axons branching from adjacent centres.
source: The barrel boundaries form a Voronoi tessellation (Senft and Woolsey, 1991; Figure 1A), suggesting that barreloid topology is preserved in the projection of thalamocortical axons into the cortex, and that a barrel forms by lateral axon branching from an initial centre-point that ceases upon contact with axons branching from adjacent centres.
evidence: This is an inference suggested by the Voronoi tessellation pattern.

claim: The assumption of pre-arranged centre-points is difficult to resolve with the observation that axons arrive in the cortical plate as an undifferentiated bundle, prior to barreloid formation.
source: However, the assumption of pre-arranged centre-points is difficult to resolve with the observation that axons arrive in the cortical plate as an undifferentiated bundle, prior to barreloid formation (Agmon et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Agmon et al., 1993.

claim: Axons arrive in the cortical plate as an undifferentiated bundle, prior to barreloid formation.
source: However, the assumption of pre-arranged centre-points is difficult to resolve with the observation that axons arrive in the cortical plate as an undifferentiated bundle, prior to barreloid formation (Agmon et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Agmon et al., 1993.

claim: In mice, axons from the trigeminal ganglion arrive in the principal division of the trigeminal nucleus (PrV) at E12.
source: In mice, axons from the trigeminal ganglion arrive in the principal division of the trigeminal nucleus (PrV) at E12, then axons from the PrV arrive in the ventroposteromedial nucleus of the thalamus (VPM) at E17, then axons from the VPM arrive in the cortical plate at E18/P0.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012 and Sehara and Kawasaki, 2011.

claim: Axons from the PrV arrive in the ventroposteromedial nucleus of the thalamus (VPM) at E17.
source: In mice, axons from the trigeminal ganglion arrive in the principal division of the trigeminal nucleus (PrV) at E12, then axons from the PrV arrive in the ventroposteromedial nucleus of the thalamus (VPM) at E17, then axons from the VPM arrive in the cortical plate at E18/P0.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012 and Sehara and Kawasaki, 2011.

claim: Axons from the VPM arrive in the cortical plate at E18/P0.
source: In mice, axons from the trigeminal ganglion arrive in the principal division of the trigeminal nucleus (PrV) at E12, then axons from the PrV arrive in the ventroposteromedial nucleus of the thalamus (VPM) at E17, then axons from the VPM arrive in the cortical plate at E18/P0.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012 and Sehara and Kawasaki, 2011.

claim: Distinct whisker-related clusters become apparent in the PrV at P0-P1.
source: Distinct whisker-related clusters then become apparent in the PrV at P0-P1, in the VPM at P2-P3, and in the cortex at P3-P5 (Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012; Sehara and Kawasaki, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012 and Sehara and Kawasaki, 2011.

claim: Distinct whisker-related clusters become apparent in the VPM at P2-P3.
source: Distinct whisker-related clusters then become apparent in the PrV at P0-P1, in the VPM at P2-P3, and in the cortex at P3-P5 (Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012; Sehara and Kawasaki, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012 and Sehara and Kawasaki, 2011.

claim: Distinct whisker-related clusters become apparent in the cortex at P3-P5.
source: Distinct whisker-related clusters then become apparent in the PrV at P0-P1, in the VPM at P2-P3, and in the cortex at P3-P5 (Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012; Sehara and Kawasaki, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Erzurumlu and Gaspar, 2012 and Sehara and Kawasaki, 2011.

claim: Karbowski and Ermentrout, 2004 developed a reaction-diffusion style model of how extrinsic signalling gradients can constrain the emergence of distinct fields from intrinsic cortical dynamics.
source: Karbowski and Ermentrout, 2004 developed a reaction-diffusion style model of how extrinsic signalling gradients can constrain the emergence of distinct fields from intrinsic cortical dynamics.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work by Karbowski and Ermentrout, 2004.

claim: All results established by Karbowski and Ermentrout, 2004 for a 1D axis could be reproduced using the extension to a 2D cortical sheet.
source: First, we verified that all results established by Karbowski and Ermentrout, 2004 for a 1D axis could be reproduced using our extension to a 2D cortical sheet.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' simulations.

claim: Localization of axon densities occurs only when projections are influenced by interactions with two or more signalling gradients that encourage migration in opposing directions.
source: This is because localization of axon densities occurs only when projections are influenced by interactions with two or more signalling gradients that encourage migration in opposing directions.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The number of guidance fields is unlikely to approach the number of individual barrels.
source: As the number of guidance fields is unlikely to approach the number of individual barrels, modifications to the model were required.
evidence: This is a reasoning based on biological plausibility.

claim: An arbitrary number of distinct field locations may be determined by a minimum of two guidance gradients if the concentration of the projection densities is influenced by competition between projections.
source: We reasoned that an arbitrary number of distinct field locations may be determined by a minimum of two guidance gradients, if the concentration of the projection densities is influenced by competition between projections, and if a projection that interacts more strongly with a given guidance gradient migrates further in the direction of that gradient.
evidence: This is a theoretical reasoning by the authors.

claim: Projections that interact most strongly with a given guidance gradient would come to occupy cortical locations at which that field has extreme values.
source: Accordingly, projections that interact most strongly with a given guidance gradient would come to occupy cortical locations at which that field has extreme values, leaving adjacent locations available to be occupied by projections with the next strongest interactions, and so forth.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the model's logic.

claim: A topological map in the cortex can be specified by a spatial ordering of the γ values at the level of the thalamus.
source: This would in principle allow the relative locations of the fields to be specified by the relative values of the interaction parameters, γ, and hence for a topological map in the cortex to be specified by a spatial ordering of the γ values at the level of the thalamus.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the model's logic.

claim: When simulated in isolation from one-another, all projections in the model would simply migrate to the extrema of the cortical guidance fields.
source: Consider, for example, that when simulated in isolation from one-another, all projections in the model described would simply migrate to the extrema of the cortical guidance fields.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' simulations.

claim: The EphA4 receptor and its ligand ephrin-A5 are distributed in complementary gradients in the somatosensory thalamus and cortex.
source: In particular, the EphA4 receptor and its ligand ephrin-A5 are distributed in complementary gradients in the somatosensory thalamus and cortex (Vanderhaeghen et al., 2000; Miller et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vanderhaeghen et al., 2000 and Miller et al., 2006.

claim: Cells originating in VPM express high levels of EphA receptors and project to the lateral part of S1, which expresses low levels of ephrin-A5.
source: Cells originating in VPM express high levels of EphA receptors and project to the lateral part of S1, which expresses low levels of ephrin-A5, and cells originating in the VPL express low levels of EphA receptors and project to the medial part of S1, which expresses high levels of ephrin-A5 (see Gao et al., 1998; Dufour et al., 2003; Vanderhaeghen and Polleux, 2004; Speer and Chapman, 2005; Torii et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cells originating in the VPL express low levels of EphA receptors and project to the medial part of S1, which expresses high levels of ephrin-A5.
source: Cells originating in VPM express high levels of EphA receptors and project to the lateral part of S1, which expresses low levels of ephrin-A5, and cells originating in the VPL express low levels of EphA receptors and project to the medial part of S1, which expresses high levels of ephrin-A5 (see Gao et al., 1998; Dufour et al., 2003; Vanderhaeghen and Polleux, 2004; Speer and Chapman, 2005; Torii et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The relative strengths of interaction with guidance molecules in the cortex are correlated with the relative concentrations of complementary molecules in the thalamus.
source: We assume that such patterning arises because the relative strengths of interaction with guidance molecules (e.g., ephrin-A5) in the cortex are correlated with the relative concentrations of complementary molecules (e.g., EphA4) in the thalamus, and thus with thalamic position along the axis to which their gradients are aligned.
evidence: This is an assumption made by the authors for their model.

claim: The shapes and arrangement of emergent connection fields came to match those of the real barrel field by around 20000 iterations.
source: A similar reduction in η in the development of the example simulation confirmed that the shapes and arrangement of emergent connection fields came to match those of the real barrel field by around 20000 iterations (Figure 1D, black squares).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The overall connection selectivity increased as the barrel map self-organized in the example simulation.
source: The overall connection selectivity increased as the barrel map self-organized in the example simulation (Figure 1D, grey hexagons), and the selectivity became concentrated in regions overlapping with the emergent barrel centres (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The selectivity became concentrated in regions overlapping with the emergent barrel centres.
source: The overall connection selectivity increased as the barrel map self-organized in the example simulation (Figure 1D, grey hexagons), and the selectivity became concentrated in regions overlapping with the emergent barrel centres (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Strongest overall connection selectivities, ω, were obtained for lower values of D.
source: Third, strongest overall connection selectivities, ω, were obtained for lower values of D.
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter sweep shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When competition is strong, the rate of diffusion determines a trade-off such that fields emerge to be barrel-shaped when diffusion is fast and they emerge to be more selectively innervated when diffusion is slow.
source: Together these results indicate that when competition is strong, the rate of diffusion determines a trade-off such that fields emerge to be barrel-shaped when diffusion is fast and they emerge to be more selectively innervated when diffusion is slow.
evidence: This is an inference from the parameter sweep results.

claim: Adding noise to the interaction parameters (γ) affected neither the Honda-δ or the connection selectivity measures substantially.
source: Adding noise to the interaction parameters (γ) affected neither the Honda-δ or the connection selectivity measures substantially (see Figure 3A), and an increase in the pattern difference reflected an increase in the occurrence of topological defects only when perturbations became so large as to cause the ordering of γ values from neighbouring thalamic sites to be switched (see example map Figure 3Bi).
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: An increase in the pattern difference reflected an increase in the occurrence of topological defects only when perturbations became so large as to cause the ordering of γ values from neighbouring thalamic sites to be switched.
source: Adding noise to the interaction parameters (γ) affected neither the Honda-δ or the connection selectivity measures substantially (see Figure 3A), and an increase in the pattern difference reflected an increase in the occurrence of topological defects only when perturbations became so large as to cause the ordering of γ values from neighbouring thalamic sites to be switched (see example map Figure 3Bi).
evidence: This is a finding from the sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3A and 3Bi.

claim: Self-organization of barrel-like fields in the model is highly robust to a wide range of sources of perturbation.
source: Overall, the sensitivity analysis revealed that self-organization of barrel-like fields in the model is highly robust to a wide range of sources of perturbation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the sensitivity analysis.

claim: Removal of whiskers by electrocauterization, plucking, or trimming leads to observable changes in brain structures, including the barrel field.
source: In a critical period comprising the first postnatal days, removal of the whiskers by electrocauterization, plucking, or trimming leads to observable changes in brain structures, including the barrel field (Jeanmonod et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jeanmonod et al., 1981.

claim: Deprivation of individual whiskers leads to smaller barrels.
source: Amongst other changes, deprivation of individual whiskers leads to smaller barrels (Kossut, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kossut, 1992.

claim: If an entire row of whiskers is trimmed, barrel sizes for the trimmed row are not obviously changed.
source: Although individual whisker trimming reduces barrel size, if an entire row is trimmed, barrel sizes for the trimmed row are not obviously changed (Land and Simons, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Land and Simons, 1985.

claim: The key requirements for the emergence of realistic barrel patterning are (i) at each cortical location thalamocortical projections compete for a limited number of available synaptic connections, (ii) at each location the branching rate of a given projection is reduced by the density of other projections, and (iii) the branch density of each projection is conserved over time.
source: The present results suggest that the key requirements for the emergence of realistic barrel patterning are (i) at each cortical location thalamocortical projections compete for a limited number of available synaptic connections (Equations 1–2), (ii) at each location the branching rate of a given projection is reduced by the density of other projections (Equation 3), and (iii) the branch density of each projection is conserved over time.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: The emergence of barrels in simulation required competition between thalamic projections in terms of synaptic connectivity and also competition in terms of cortical space.
source: The emergence of barrels in simulation required competition between thalamic projections in terms of synaptic connectivity and also competition in terms of cortical space, as represented by χ, with an implicit requirement for a self/other identifier amongst projections.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Competition for cortical space requires an implicit self/other identifier amongst projections.
source: The emergence of barrels in simulation required competition between thalamic projections in terms of synaptic connectivity and also competition in terms of cortical space, as represented by χ, with an implicit requirement for a self/other identifier amongst projections.
evidence: This is an inference from the model structure.

claim: Competition for space may account for the absence of barrels in rodents with larger brains, such as capybara.
source: This latter form of competition may account for the absence of barrels in rodents with larger brains, such as capybara, for which competition for space is presumably weaker (Woolsey et al., 1975).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model and supported by a citation to Woolsey et al., 1975.

claim: The emergence of somatotopically ordered modular structures may be an inevitable consequence of local competition for cortical territory driven by input from an array of discrete sensory organs.
source: Hence, irrespective of whether barrels are necessary for adaptive whisker function, the emergence of somatotopically ordered modular structures may be an inevitable consequence of local competition for cortical territory driven by input from an array of discrete sensory organs (Purves et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model results and supported by a citation to Purves et al., 1992.

claim: The Voronoi tessellation is extended by scores of smaller barrels alongside the E-row barrels, which represent the microvibrissae.
source: In reality, the Voronoi tessellation is extended by scores of smaller barrels alongside the E-row barrels, which represent the microvibrissae, and presumably form via the same competitive processes.
evidence: This is a statement about biological reality.

claim: Smaller barrels representing the microvibrissae presumably form via the same competitive processes as the macrovibrissae barrels.
source: In reality, the Voronoi tessellation is extended by scores of smaller barrels alongside the E-row barrels, which represent the microvibrissae, and presumably form via the same competitive processes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the model.

claim: The formulation of the model is entirely local, insofar as simulation requires no information to be communicated from a given cortical grid cell to any but those immediately adjacent.
source: It is important to emphasize that the formulation of the model is entirely local, insofar as simulation requires no information to be communicated from a given cortical grid cell to any but those immediately adjacent (via diffusion).
evidence: This is a description of the model's properties.

claim: The simulations demonstrate how a self-organizing system, constrained by genetically specified guidance cues and by the shape of the cortical field boundary, can faithfully reproduce an arrangement of cell aggregates in one neural structure as a topographic map in another.
source: Hence the simulations demonstrate how a self-organizing system, constrained by genetically specified guidance cues and by the shape of the cortical field boundary, can faithfully reproduce an arrangement of cell aggregates in one neural structure as a topographic map in another.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Somatotopic map formation does not require the pre-specification of centre-points by as yet undetermined additional developmental mechanisms.
source: Moreover, the present results confirm that somatotopic map formation does not require the pre-specification of centre-points by as yet undetermined additional developmental mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: The cortical sheet was modelled as a two dimensional hexagonal lattice.
source: The cortical sheet was modelled as a two dimensional hexagonal lattice, which simplifies the computation of the 2D Laplacian.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling method.

claim: A hexagonal lattice simplifies the computation of the 2D Laplacian.
source: The cortical sheet was modelled as a two dimensional hexagonal lattice, which simplifies the computation of the 2D Laplacian.
evidence: This is a statement about computational methods.

claim: The hex-to-hex distance d was set to 0.03 mm.
source: Within a boundary traced around the edge of a rat barrel field (Figure 1A) we set the hex-to-hex distance d to 0.03 mm, which resulted in a lattice containing 6515 hexes for the simulations shown in Figure 1A,C and D and 12739 hexes for the Fgf8 misexpression study shown in Figure 3.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling parameters.

claim: The lattice contained 6515 hexes for the simulations shown in Figure 1A,C and D.
source: Within a boundary traced around the edge of a rat barrel field (Figure 1A) we set the hex-to-hex distance d to 0.03 mm, which resulted in a lattice containing 6515 hexes for the simulations shown in Figure 1A,C and D and 12739 hexes for the Fgf8 misexpression study shown in Figure 3.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling parameters.

claim: The lattice contained 12739 hexes for the Fgf8 misexpression study shown in Figure 3.
source: Within a boundary traced around the edge of a rat barrel field (Figure 1A) we set the hex-to-hex distance d to 0.03 mm, which resulted in a lattice containing 6515 hexes for the simulations shown in Figure 1A,C and D and 12739 hexes for the Fgf8 misexpression study shown in Figure 3.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling parameters (note: likely Figure 4 based on context).

claim: Each hex contained 82 time-dependent variables: 41 branching densities (ai) and 41 connection densities (ci).
source: Each hex contained 82 time-dependent variables: 41 branching densities (ai) and 41 connection densities (ci).
evidence: This is a description of the modeling structure.

claim: The rate of change of each of the time-dependent variables was computed using a fourth-order Runge-Kutta method.
source: The rate of change of each of the time-dependent variables (Equations 1 and 2) was computed using a fourth-order Runge-Kutta method.
evidence: This is a description of the computational method.
